title: Abba (Mark 14:32–42)
hookLine: in Gethsemane he calls God Abba, Father, and asks for the cup to pass

cards: After supper they go out to the Mount of Olives, to a place called Gethsemane. Tradition says the name means oil press, the place where olives are crushed.

Jesus tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, and takes Peter, James and John a little further. Then Mark says something about Jesus you haven't heard before: he began to be deeply distressed and troubled.
He tells them, in the King James Bible: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death: tarry ye here, and watch." He goes a little further on alone, and falls on the ground. Not kneeling, composed.
On the ground. And the first word out of his mouth is today's word.

teach.b: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is an Aramaic word. Mark keeps it, then translates it for his Greek readers: Father.
You may have heard that abba means daddy. Mark doesn't say that; he gives it simply as Father. And Paul, writing in Greek to grown men and women, keeps the word too: they cry Abba, Father.
So whatever else it is, it isn't baby talk. It's family talk, said by a son in the dark. Listen to the whole prayer.
All things are possible to you: the same words he gave the father of the boy, and the disciples at the needle's eye.

teach.h: TAKE THIS CUP, YET THY WILL.
teach.b: Take away this cup: Isaiah speaks of a cup of trembling. Then the turn: not what I will, but what you will. He asks honestly for what he wants, then hands it over.
He comes back, and they're asleep.

teach.h: COULDEST NOT THOU WATCH ONE HOUR?
teach.b: "Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?" Watch, the word from a few days ago. "The spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak."
He goes and prays the same words again. Comes back: asleep. A third time.

teach.h: NOT WHAT I WILL, BUT WHAT THOU WILT.
teach.b: Then: it is enough. The hour has come. Rise up, let's go.
Many Christians see here both how human Jesus was and how he trusted. In the dark, face down, he still says Abba.

how: Many Christians pray Jesus's words "not what I will, but what thou wilt" in times of struggle, and some churches keep a watch of prayer late on Maundy Thursday night in memory of Gethsemane.

o: master, a respectful word for a teacher
father, the word a child uses at home
daddy, baby talk for a little child

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Mark translates it simply as Father, and Paul uses it for grown believers.
Paul, writing in Greek, still uses the word abba
Jesus prayed only once in Gethsemane
he prayed three times, and found them asleep each time.

games.q: you're Jesus, face down in the olive grove, knowing what's coming. what do you pray?
o: give me strength to bear it.
Abba, take this cup; yet not my will, but yours.
games.why: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt."

practice: Think of what you'd say if you could be completely honest with someone who loves you: what do you want taken away, and what are you afraid of?
If you pray, speak to God the way Jesus did, Abba, Father, say plainly what you want, and then, only if you can, add his next words: nevertheless, not what I will, but what thou wilt.
If you don't pray, just let yourself be honest, like a child would be.

wordCard.voice: Abba. Aramaic for father, the word a child uses at home. Jesus's first word in Gethsemane.

orig.note: Aramaic for father, written in Greek letters in Mark 14:36, then translated: ho patēr.

carryVoice: Your line: abba, father. Honest words, said face down in the dark at Gethsemane. Until tomorrow.
